definitions.definition: Complex exponential smoothing: a forecasting method that combines each past observation $y_t$ and its forecast error $e_t$ into the complex variable $y_t + i e_t$ and forecasts with an exponentially weighted sum of these values, the weights being powers of $1 + i - (\alpha_0 + i\alpha_1)$ times the complex smoothing parameter $\alpha_0 + i\alpha_1$.

The smoothing parameter of CES, the complex number $\alpha_0 + i\alpha_1$; its real part $\alpha_0$ and imaginary part $\alpha_1$ are the two real parameters estimated, and they set how much of the past observations and of the past forecast errors is carried into the forecast.

The state $c_t$ of the CES state-space model, which carries information on both its own previous value $c_{t-1}$ and the previous level $l_{t-1}$; it does not correspond to the trend component of exponential smoothing.

CES extended with a second pair of level and nonlinear trend states taken at lag $m$, the seasonal period, with its own complex smoothing parameter $\beta_0 + i\beta_1$: $y_t = l_{0,t-1} + l_{1,t-m} + \varepsilon_t$, where $l_{0,t}, c_{0,t}$ follow the non-seasonal CES equations at lag 1 and $l_{1,t}, c_{1,t}$ the same equations at lag $m$.
Simple combination of univariate models: the median of the forecasts of ETS, ARIMA, the Theta method and CES.
The median of the forecasts of ETS, ARIMA and the Theta method: SCUM without CES.
The 5,315 yearly, quarterly, monthly and other time series of the M1, M3 and tourism forecasting competitions.
Exponential smoothing in a state space framework with automatic selection among its models; here es() from the smooth package with model ZXZ, selecting by AICc.
Automatic state space ARIMA; here auto.ssarima() from the smooth package.
The Theta method of forecasting; here thetaf() from the forecast package 8.14.

Root mean squared scaled error: the root mean squared forecast error over the horizon, scaled by the mean absolute first difference of the in-sample data; reported as its mean and median over the series.
Mean absolute scaled error: the mean absolute forecast error over the horizon, scaled by the mean absolute first difference of the in-sample data; reported as its mean and median over the series.

Mean scaled interval score: the interval score of a prediction interval averaged over the horizon and scaled by the mean absolute first difference of the in-sample data; here of the 95% prediction interval, reported as its mean and median over the series.
CES fitted by auto.ces() from the smooth package 3.1.2, which chooses between seasonal and non-seasonal CES by AICc.
The ETS models ETS(A,N,N), ETS(A,A,N), ETS(A,Ad,N), ETS(M,M,N) and ETS(M,Md,N), each fitted without model selection.
The ETS models ETS(A,N,A), ETS(A,A,A), ETS(A,Ad,A), ETS(M,M,M) and ETS(M,Md,M), each fitted without model selection.

The 100,000 series of the M4 competition (23,000 yearly, 24,000 quarterly, 48,000 monthly, 359 weekly, 4,227 daily and 414 hourly) except series 19357, 43160, 51552, 62738, 92370, 92435, 93159, 93196, 93412 and 93491, whose influential outliers and structural breaks made ETS break down.
The 3,262 series of the M1, M3 and tourism data for which ETS model selection by es() from the smooth package chooses a non-seasonal model.
The 2,053 series of the M1, M3 and tourism data for which ETS model selection by es() from the smooth package chooses a seasonal model.

A criterion for choosing among models fitted by maximum likelihood that penalises the maximised log-likelihood by the number of estimated parameters.
Augmented Dickey-Fuller test of the null hypothesis that a time series has a unit root.
Kwiatkowski-Phillips-Schmidt-Shin test of the null hypothesis that a time series is stationary.

claims.statement: Depending on the value of its [[D2:complex smoothing parameter]], [[D1:CES]] is a stationary or a non-stationary model.

relations.note: Exponential smoothing in a state space framework (ETS) gives 30 models with no, additive or multiplicative error, trend and seasonal components, among which a model is selected by an information criterion.
Identifying the presence and type of trend in exponential smoothing often leads to misidentification and poorly performing long-term forecasts.
The diverse trend alternatives of exponential smoothing in a state space framework make the selection of a model difficult.
Selecting the most appropriate exponential smoothing model is a challenging task.
Even when the components of exponential smoothing are identified correctly, the estimated smoothing parameters and the weights they imply can give poor forecasts.

claims.statement: [[D1:CES]] passes continuously from a stationary to a non-stationary model as its [[D2:complex smoothing parameter]] changes.

[[D1:CES]] has an underlying ARMA(2,2) model whose coefficients $\phi_1 = 2 - \alpha_0$, $\phi_2 = \alpha_0 + \alpha_1 - 2$, $\theta_1 = 2 - 2\alpha_0 + \alpha_1$ and $\theta_2 = 3\alpha_0 + \alpha_1 - 2 - \alpha_0^2 - \alpha_1^2$ are nonlinear functions of the same two parameters $\alpha_0$ and $\alpha_1$.
The parameter space of the ARMA(2,2) model underlying [[D1:CES]] differs from that of the general ARMA(2,2) model.
The parameter space of the ARMA(2,2) model underlying [[D1:CES]] is not restricted to stationary models.
[[D4:seasonal CES]] models seasonality with lag-$m$ level and nonlinear trend states instead of seasonal indices.
[[D4:seasonal CES]] has no seasonal indices that need renormalising.
Model selection for [[D1:CES]] reduces to choosing between the seasonal and the non-seasonal model.
On the [[D7:M1, M3 and tourism data]], [[D5:SCUM]] has lower mean and median [[D11:RMSSE]] and [[D12:MASE]] and lower median [[D13:MSIS]] than [[D6:SCUM(noCES)]], but higher mean MSIS.

scope.population: time series of the M1, M3 and tourism forecasting competitions

claims.statement: [[D1:CES]] has the single-source-of-error state-space form $y_t = l_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t$, $l_t = l_{t-1} - (1 - \alpha_1) c_{t-1} + (\alpha_0 - \alpha_1) \varepsilon_t$, $c_t = l_{t-1} + (1 - \alpha_0) c_{t-1} + (\alpha_0 + \alpha_1) \varepsilon_t$, with level $l_t$ and [[D3:nonlinear trend component]] $c_t$, whose transition matrix contains the smoothing parameters.
The [[D23:Akaike information criterion]] of seasonal and non-seasonal [[D1:CES]] can be computed from a Gaussian likelihood of the same form as that of additive exponential smoothing models.
[[D1:CES]] is stationary, with both eigenvalues of its transition matrix inside the unit circle, when $\alpha_1 < 5 - 2\alpha_0$, $\alpha_1 < 1$ and $\alpha_1 > 1 - \alpha_0$.
When $\alpha_1 > 1$, both eigenvalues of the [[D1:CES]] transition matrix are real and one of them is greater than one.
When $\alpha_1 > 1$, [[D1:CES]] produces a non-stationary trajectory.
When $\alpha_1 = 1$, [[D1:CES]] is equivalent to ETS(A,N,N).

[[D1:CES]] is stable, with all eigenvalues of its discount matrix inside the unit circle, when $(\alpha_0 - 2.5)^2 + \alpha_1^2 > 1.25$, $(\alpha_0 - 0.5)^2 + (\alpha_1 - 1)^2 > 0.25$ and $(\alpha_0 - 1.5)^2 + (\alpha_1 - 0.5)^2 < 1.5$.
The stable region of [[D1:CES]] contains both stationary and non-stationary values of the [[D2:complex smoothing parameter]].

The [[D1:CES]] point forecast $w'F^{h-1}v_t$ follows one of five trajectories set by the [[D2:complex smoothing parameter]]: a flat line, exponential growth, exponential decline, harmonic oscillation converging to zero, or diverging harmonic oscillation.
When $\alpha_1 = 1$, the [[D1:CES]] point forecast is a flat line.
When $\alpha_1 > 1$, the [[D1:CES]] point forecast grows exponentially.
When $(4 - \alpha_0^2)/4 < \alpha_1 < 1$, the [[D1:CES]] point forecast declines exponentially.
When $1 - \alpha_0 < \alpha_1 < (4 - \alpha_0^2)/4$, the [[D1:CES]] point forecast is a harmonic oscillation converging to zero.
When $0 < \alpha_1 < 1 - \alpha_0$, the [[D1:CES]] point forecast is a diverging harmonic oscillation.
The conditional variance of [[D1:CES]] $h$ steps ahead, given the level and the nonlinear trend component, can be calculated from its state-space form in the same way as for pure additive ETS models.
On M3 series 1664, which graphical analysis and [[D24:ADF test]] and [[D25:KPSS test]] indicate is stationary, [[D1:CES]] estimates the stationary $\alpha_0 + i\alpha_1 = 0.99999 + 0.99884i$.
On M3 series 1664, all holdout observations lie inside the 95% prediction interval of [[D1:CES]].
[[D4:seasonal CES]] has an underlying SARIMA(2,0,2m+2)(2,0,0)$_m$ model.
[[D4:seasonal CES]] can produce seasonality whose amplitude changes nonlinearly.
[[D4:seasonal CES]] can produce all the trajectories of non-seasonal [[D1:CES]].
[[D4:seasonal CES]] can model multiplicative or other shapes of seasonality when the level of the series does not change.
Non-seasonal [[D1:CES]] has 5 estimated parameters: two smoothing parameters, two initial states and the error variance.
[[D4:seasonal CES]] has $4 + 2m + 2 + 1$ estimated parameters: four smoothing parameters, $2m$ initial lagged values, two initial non-seasonal states and the error variance.

On the [[D7:M1, M3 and tourism data]], CES has the lowest mean [[D11:RMSSE]] and the lowest median RMSSE, [[D12:MASE]] and [[D13:MSIS]] of four methods, CES, [[D8:ETS]], [[D9:ARIMA]] and the [[D10:Theta method]], but not the lowest mean MASE, and the highest mean MSIS.

[[D1:CES]] encompasses level processes.
[[D1:CES]] encompasses multiplicative trend processes.
[[D1:CES]] approximates additive trend processes well.
When $\alpha_1$ is close to 1, [[D1:CES]] behaves like simple exponential smoothing with smoothing parameter $\alpha_0 - 1$.

When $\alpha_1$ is close to 1, the real part $\alpha_0$ of the complex smoothing parameter of [[D1:CES]] is close to 1 for a stationary series, for which the smoothing parameter of simple exponential smoothing would be close to 0.

warrants.text: The seasonal model takes the level and nonlinear trend states at lag m instead of carrying a set of seasonal components, so there are no seasonal indices to renormalise. Since non-seasonal CES captures both level and trend series without a choice of trend form, the only choice left is whether to include the lag-m states.

Seasonal CES consists of two CES parts, one at lag 1 and one at lag m, and each part follows one of the CES forecast trajectories, so the seasonal part can grow, decline or oscillate in its own way. The non-seasonal level can become negative while the lagged level stays positive, and the two levels evolve independently, so the seasonal part can change its amplitude and shape without any change in the level of the series.

The count follows from the model equations: each complex smoothing parameter has two real parts, each pair of level and nonlinear trend states needs initial values (m of each for the lag-m pair), and the error variance is estimated.

With the imaginary part of the smoothing parameter equal to one CES is the local level model ETS(A,N,N); with it above one the forecasts grow exponentially, as in multiplicative trend models; and the flexibility of its trajectories lets it follow trends that the level and trend classification of exponential smoothing captures only with separate models.

On the seasonal subset of the M1, M3 and tourism data, CES with its seasonal or non-seasonal form chosen by AICc has lower RMSSE and MASE than every seasonal ETS model, which the authors take to show that the criterion chooses the seasonal form when it is needed. This is an argument from the accuracy results only: no experiment compares the selection by information criteria with other ways of choosing between seasonal and non-seasonal CES.

CES has lower RMSSE than ETS, ARIMA and the Theta method on the M1, M3, tourism and M4 data and lowers the errors of the combination it is included in, which the authors take as evidence that it is robust, while acknowledging that it does not suit every forecasting scenario. Robustness itself is not defined or tested: no experiment examines how the accuracy of CES varies across conditions or departures from its assumptions.

CES, which has no separate trend forms, has lower RMSSE than ETS, which selects among trend forms, on competition data that contain both level and trended series, which the authors take to validate that CES handles both kinds of series by its smooth transition between trajectories. No experiment separates level from trended series to test this: the comparison is on the pooled competition data.

Non-seasonal CES has an underlying ARMA(2,2) model that is stationary or not depending on its complex smoothing parameter; by analogy, the authors state the same of the SARIMA model underlying seasonal CES. No stationarity condition is derived for seasonal CES.

limitations.statement: CES produces very large errors on a few series: on M1 series 47 it fails to identify the trend and its MSIS is 523.034 against 25.590 for ETS(M,N,N), which inflates its mean MSIS, and on the non-seasonal subset it fails on two series.
The parameter restrictions under which seasonal CES is stable are not derived.
The effect of the length of a time series on the accuracy of CES is not analysed.
CES is formulated only with an additive error term; a version with a multiplicative error term is not developed.
The 10 M4 series on which ETS broke down were excluded from the M4 comparison, so the series were selected on the failure of one of the compared methods.
